Calibration of a prediction against observed outcomes

Source: R/ilm_calibration.R
ilm_calibration.ilm_pred.Rd

Whether outcomes fell where their predictive distributions said they would: coverage and width level by level, bias in the mean, and the uniformity of the probability integral transforms (PITs; Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery 2007, section 3.1, pp. 251-253). A binary outcome is judged instead by its calibration intercept and slope, which together assess what Van Calster et al. (2019, p. 4) call weak calibration. The result ends with a verdict in plain words and, where something is wrong, a remedy that exists, most often in illume.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'ilm_pred'
ilm_calibration(
  object,
  y,
  bins = 10L,
  levels = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95),
  seed = 1L,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A prediction from ilm_predict() or ilm_forecast() with target = "response".

y

The observed outcomes, one per row of the prediction. At least 20 must be scoreable.

bins

The number of bins for the PIT's uniformity test, and for a binary outcome's reliability table. There are fewer when the outcomes are few.

levels

The central interval levels at which coverage is checked.

seed

The seed for the randomised PITs of a discrete outcome. The caller's random-number state is left as it was.

...

Unused.

Value

An object of class "ilm_pred_calibration", a list:

  • pit, each row's PIT;

  • n, the outcomes used;

  • histogram and uniformity;

  • bias;

  • coverage, a data frame of level, coverage, its standard error and mean width;

  • family;

  • for a binary outcome, binary (the intercept and slope) and reliability;

  • checks, the diagnostics as data;

  • verdict, their words as printed.

ilm_plot_calibration() draws it.

Details

This is limn's method for illume's illume::ilm_calibration() generic, for a prediction. illume's own method checks a fitted model's category probabilities.

What is checked

  • Coverage and width. At each level in levels, the share of outcomes inside the central interval of their predictive distributions, with its standard error, and the intervals' mean width. Coverage is read from the PITs, not from whether the outcome lies inside a quantile interval. A discrete outcome's quantile interval covers more than its level, because of ties, while the randomised PIT's coverage is exactly nominal when the model is right.

  • Bias, on the outcome's own scale: the mean of the outcome minus its predictive mean, with its standard error. The mean PIT is not used, since a distribution with the right mean and the wrong shape moves it too.

  • PIT uniformity: a chi-square test over bins equal bins, with at least 5 outcomes expected in each (limn's choice of minimum).

  • A binary outcome: the calibration intercept (are the probabilities right on average?) and slope (are they too extreme, or too moderate?), with Wald 95% intervals, and a reliability table of equal-count bins with Wilson intervals. Interval coverage adds nothing for a 0/1 outcome.

A coverage or bias departure is called when it is more than 2.58 standard errors from its ideal (the two-sided 99% point of the normal distribution, limn's own choice), and a binary measure when its 95% interval excludes the ideal. The intercept's ideal is 0 and the slope's is 1 (Van Calster et al. 2019, p. 4).

A biased mean is reported first. It alone can make the intervals cover too little, since they are centred in the wrong place. So a shortfall in coverage beside it is reported as one the bias can cause, and the remedies that widen intervals wait until the mean is fixed. A calibration slope whose interval lies wholly below 0 is reported as reversed, a verdict of limn's own: the predictions order the outcomes the wrong way, which is more than being too extreme.

Verdicts

What each check means and what to do about it, in the words it is printed with. A reference supports what was found and why; a remedy draws on it only where it says so, and anything marked as limn's own reasoning is not the source's:

  • bias (warn): Biased: outcomes are on average some amount above or below their predicted means (SE s). The mean structure is missing something the outcomes follow. illume::ilm_remedies() and illume's residual checks point at which term.

  • coverage (warn): Too narrow: a share of outcomes fell inside the central L% of their predictive distributions, against L% expected. A biased mean alone can cause this: the intervals are centred in the wrong place. Fix the mean first, as above, then check the coverage again; widen the intervals only if it still falls short.

  • coverage (warn): Too narrow: a share of outcomes fell inside the central L% of their predictive distributions, against L% expected. The predictions are more certain than the data bear out. Reference: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery (2007), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 69, 243-268, pp. 252-253. Overdispersion is the usual cause for counts (limn's own reasoning): refit with family = "nbinom" in illume::ilm_model(), which lets the variance exceed the mean.

  • coverage (warn): Too narrow: a share of outcomes fell inside the central L% of their predictive distributions, against L% expected. The predictions are more certain than the data bear out. Reference: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery (2007), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 69, 243-268, pp. 252-253. Let the dispersion vary with the predictors through a dispformula in illume::ilm_model(); with few groups and predictions for new units, refit with reml = TRUE.

  • coverage (warn): Too narrow: a share of outcomes fell inside the central L% of their predictive distributions, against L% expected. The predictions are more certain than the data bear out. Reference: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery (2007), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 69, 243-268, pp. 252-253. illume::ilm_remedies() lists the model changes the fit's own checks support, and illume::ilm_apply_remedy() refits the model with the one you choose.

  • coverage (warn): Too wide: a share of outcomes fell inside the central L% of their predictive distributions, against L% expected. The predictions are less certain than the data show. Reference: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery (2007), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 69, 243-268, pp. 252-253. An overdispersed family, or a dispersion model the data do not need, widens every interval (limn's own reasoning): illume::ilm_remedies() lists the model changes the fit's own checks support, and illume::ilm_apply_remedy() refits the model with the one you choose.

  • calibration (ok): Consistent with calibration: coverage within sampling error at every level, no bias in the mean, and the PITs consistent with uniform (p).

  • calibration intercept (warn): Off on average: a share of outcomes were 1, against another predicted; the calibration intercept is b (95% interval l to u). The probabilities are too high or too low overall. Reference: Van Calster and others (2019), BMC Medicine 17, 230, pp. 2 and 4. A difference between the data the model was fitted to and the data scored, such as a different rate of the outcome, can cause this (the reference, p. 2): illume::ilm_remedies() lists the model changes the fit's own checks support, and illume::ilm_apply_remedy() refits the model with the one you choose.

  • calibration slope (warn): Reversed: the calibration slope is b (95% interval l to u); the predictions order the outcomes the wrong way. This verdict is limn's own: the reference defines the calibration slope, with a target of 1, and reads a slope below 1 as too extreme, but does not discuss one below 0. Outcomes the model rates more likely turn out less likely; it may have fitted noise, or the scored data may differ from the data it was fitted to (limn's own reasoning). Reference: Van Calster and others (2019), BMC Medicine 17, 230, p. 4. Use fewer terms, or penalised ones: smooths in illume::ilm_model() are penalised; and check that the scored data come from the same population and coding.

  • calibration slope (warn): Overconfident: the calibration slope is b (95% interval l to u); predicted probabilities are too extreme. The model has fitted noise, so its probabilities stray too far from the average. Reference: Van Calster and others (2019), BMC Medicine 17, 230, pp. 2 and 4. Use fewer terms, or penalised ones (the reference, p. 4): smooths in illume::ilm_model() are penalised.

  • calibration slope (warn): Underconfident: the calibration slope is b (95% interval l to u); predicted probabilities are too moderate. The probabilities stay too close to the average. Reference: Van Calster and others (2019), BMC Medicine 17, 230, p. 4. A penalty stronger than the data warrant can cause this (limn's own reasoning): illume::ilm_remedies() lists the model changes the fit's own checks support, and illume::ilm_apply_remedy() refits the model with the one you choose.

  • calibration (ok): Consistent with calibration: the calibration intercept includes 0 and the slope includes 1.

The rows are treated as independent

Rows that share a group, a series or a forecast origin are not independent, and then the standard errors and tests here are too confident. For forecasts, check calibration horizon by horizon, or over rows from different series and origins.

References

Gneiting, T., Balabdaoui, F. and Raftery, A. E. (2007). Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 69, 243-268. Section 3.1, pp. 251-253: the PIT, its uniformity, coverage read from it, and the histogram's shapes.

Van Calster, B., McLernon, D. J., van Smeden, M., Wynants, L. and Steyerberg, E. W. (2019). Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics. BMC Medicine 17, 230. p. 2: causes of poor calibration; p. 4: weak calibration, the intercept and slope and their targets, and remedies.

See also

ilm_pit(), ilm_plot_calibration(), ilm_scores.ilm_pred()

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(400))
d$y <- rnbinom(400, size = 1.5, mu = exp(1 + 0.5 * d$x))
train <- d[1:200, ]; test <- d[201:400, ]
## Poisson on overdispersed counts: intervals too narrow, and the remedy
fp <- illume::ilm_model(y ~ x, data = train, family = "poisson", verbose = FALSE)
illume::ilm_calibration(ilm_predict(fp, test, target = "response", nsim = 200), test$y)
#> <calibration> 200 outcomes, poisson predictive distributions
#>   PIT uniformity: chi-square 53.7 on 9 df, p < 0.001
#>   coverage by level (from the PITs):
#>      50%:  35.5% (SE 3.54 percentage points), mean width 2.15
#>      80%:  61.5% (SE 2.83 percentage points), mean width 4.10
#>      90%:  75.5% (SE 2.12 percentage points), mean width 5.17
#>      95%:  81.0% (SE 1.54 percentage points), mean width 6.05
#>   Too narrow: 81.0% of outcomes fell inside the central 95% of their predictive distributions, against 95% expected. The predictions are more certain than the data bear out. Reference: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery (2007), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 69, 243-268, pp. 252-253.
#>   Remedy: Overdispersion is the usual cause for counts (limn's own reasoning): refit with family = "nbinom" in illume::ilm_model(), which lets the variance exceed the mean.
## the negative binomial the verdict names
fn <- illume::ilm_model(y ~ x, data = train, family = "nbinom", verbose = FALSE)
illume::ilm_calibration(ilm_predict(fn, test, target = "response", nsim = 200), test$y)
#> <calibration> 200 outcomes, nbinom predictive distributions
#>   PIT uniformity: chi-square 14.6 on 9 df, p = 0.103
#>   coverage by level (from the PITs):
#>      50%:  54.0% (SE 3.54 percentage points), mean width 3.31
#>      80%:  82.5% (SE 2.83 percentage points), mean width 6.42
#>      90%:  91.5% (SE 2.12 percentage points), mean width 8.25
#>      95%:  97.0% (SE 1.54 percentage points), mean width 10.1
#>   Consistent with calibration: coverage within sampling error at every level, no bias in the mean, and the PITs consistent with uniform (p = 0.103).
